title: Community-Defined Microgrid Resilience Across Interdependent Services and Changing Climate Conditions
summary: How can communities design renewable microgrids to protect the services they value most during outages, now and as the climate changes?
overview: Microgrids are increasingly central to both resilience policy and decarbonization strategy, yet prevailing planning methods size them around expert-defined loads and fixed outage scenarios. These methods can overlook community priorities, the risk that disruption to one service will affect others, and uncertainty about future conditions. This project aims to close that gap so resilience investments protect the services and people that communities value most while supporting the shift to clean energy.

approach.title: Identify critical services with communities
approach.text: Capture community-defined critical services, dependencies, and priorities, and translate them into validated inputs for a socio-technical network and a microgrid techno-economic model.

approach.title: Test designs during outages
approach.text: Evaluate how candidate designs sustain prioritized loads and services during outages, limit cascading failures, and improve community resilience.

approach.title: Compare investments over the microgrid lifetime
approach.text: Evaluate how those benefits change under future climate-driven demand, solar, and outage conditions, and compare investment strategies for preserving performance across the microgrid lifetime.

expectedOutcomes: The project will produce a planning criterion that communities can use to direct microgrid investment toward the services they most want to protect. It will give planners, utilities, and funders a transparent, reusable way to evaluate investments that accounts for how failures spread across infrastructure. By making the long-term protective value of renewable microgrids explicit, the research can support greater use of low-carbon generation and storage in place of fossil-fuel backup.
funding: Alfred P. Sloan Foundation · Early-Career Faculty Support for Interdisciplinary Energy Systems Research

title: SEER — Sustainable Electricity Expansion Roadmaps
summary: Democratizing power systems planning for a robust and sustainable energy transition.
overview: Power system planning shapes investments in generation and grid infrastructure. Fragmented data and inaccessible tools can limit participation in these decisions, particularly in the Global South. SEER aims to make planning faster, more flexible, and more accessible to energy-sector stakeholders.

The project is developing an open dataset to support machine learning approaches, including automated input-data generation and models that approximate optimization solvers. Collaboration with planning practitioners is central to making the tools useful for real decisions.

title: The role of electric boiling in the electric cooking transition in Nairobi and Kigali
summary: Investigating the role of electric boiling in the electric cooking transition in Nairobi and Kigali
overview: Investigating the role of electric boiling in the electric cooking transition in Nairobi and Kigali.

In Summer 2025, Eliane Nirere led data collection in Kigali to assess household electricity and cooking-fuel use. She designed the KoboToolbox survey, trained 20 enumerators, and led fieldwork with more than 2,000 households across six sectors. She also led household selection and the distribution of more than 350 kettles to low-electricity-consuming households to assess electric water boiling as a convenient, affordable alternative for cooking tasks.

title: CORE — Community Owned Renewable Electrification
summary: Research and collaboration on community-owned renewable electrification in Nigeria.
overview: The Community-Owned Renewable Electrification (CORE) project supported Nigeria’s Rural Electrification Agency (REA) to develop, test, and scale a community-led model for renewable electricity service provision. Through this model, known as the Renewable Energy Users’ Cooperative Societies (REUCS), communities took ownership of mini-grid operations, governance, and long-term sustainability.

CORE was implemented by a consortium led by Mercy Corps – Energy 4 Impact, together with local partner Murty International and the Kigali Collaborative Research Centre (KCRC). The consortium brought together complementary expertise to strengthen and expand the REUCS model nationwide.

title: Spotlight Kampala
summary: Community-engaged research on electricity access, service quality, and electric cooking in Kampala’s informal settlements.
overview: Spotlight Kampala brings Ugandan and international researchers together with residents to understand and improve electricity services in informal settlements. Its research connects infrastructure, affordability, safety, and community priorities.

The collaboration surveyed 500 households, conducted 66 interviews, deployed 148 remote power-quality sensors, and mapped infrastructure across 25 communities. Findings were returned to participating communities to help identify priority solutions.

Electric cooking research combines household engagement, monitoring, and wiring inspections. More recent work explores community-designed solar cooking systems and payment, ownership, and maintenance arrangements.

title: User-centered design to promote electric cooking transitions in informal settlements
summary: Testing solar-powered electric cooking systems with Kampala households to understand usability, reliability, affordability, and pathways to sustained adoption.
overview: In collaboration with Spotlight Kampala, Makerere University, and the University of California, Berkeley, this project examines user-centered approaches to electric cooking in Kampala’s informal settlements. The MECS-STARSS pilot ran from September 2025 to February 2026, with implementation partners ACTogether Uganda and the National Slum Dwellers Federation of Uganda.

The pilot tested standalone solar photovoltaic systems paired with electric pressure cookers, an electric pressure cooker battery-swapping service, and ECOCA’s integrated solar cooking system. Household deployment combined technical monitoring, surveys, and qualitative feedback.

The final report identifies battery reliability, accessible local technical support, practical installation, and flexible financing as priorities for sustained adoption. It highlights strong household interest alongside challenges related to charging, equipment handling, limited space, and affordability.
funding: Modern Energy Cooking Services (MECS) Programme · MECS-STARSS · UKAid

title: Community Benefit Agreements in Utility-Scale Energy Projects
summary: Examining how U.S. community benefit agreements for utility-scale energy projects define, deliver, and enforce benefits across rural, urban, and tribal communities. Case studies document negotiation, accountability, community engagement, and implementation challenges.
overview: Examining how U.S. community benefit agreements for utility-scale energy projects define, deliver, and enforce benefits across rural, urban, and tribal communities. Case studies document negotiation, accountability, community engagement, and implementation challenges.
objectives: Compile U.S. case studies of community benefit agreements (CBAs) for utility-scale energy projects across rural, urban, and tribal communities.
Compare agreement structures, negotiating parties, and terms, with emphasis on how benefits are defined and enforced through responsibilities, reporting, and penalties for non-compliance.
Identify best practices for early, transparent engagement, inclusive decision-making, community priorities, and accountability.
Examine barriers to negotiation and implementation, including trust, information gaps, confidentiality, power imbalances, and enforcement.
Document state and federal policies that encourage or require community benefits, including the Department of Energy’s Community Benefits Plan requirement.

title: Longitudinal assessment of rooftop solar adoption in Seattle
summary: Tracking rooftop solar adoption and untapped rooftop potential across Seattle’s census tracts to understand who benefits and which communities are left behind.
overview: This project tracks how rooftop solar has spread across Seattle’s census tracts over time. It compares where solar has been installed with where rooftops could support it, showing how much of each area’s solar potential has been used. It then looks at how these patterns line up with income, race, homeownership, and other measures of community vulnerability. The goal is to identify which communities have shared in the benefits of rooftop solar and which have been left behind.

title: Community Microgrid Resilience Under Intensifying Climate Conditions
summary: Examining how intensifying climate change affects the resilience benefits of community solar and storage microgrids in the Pacific Northwest.
overview: Aya Alayli’s study is a subproject of the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation–supported project “Community-Defined Microgrid Resilience Across Interdependent Services and Changing Climate Conditions.”

This research examines the long-term resilience performance of solar and storage systems under intensifying climate conditions. Following exploratory work in Spring 2025, Aya developed a microgrid dispatch simulation to evaluate resilience under uncertain climate conditions.
In Autumn 2026, the work expanded to consider interdependent community services, alongside preparatory work for participatory research with Washington communities.
